title: BEFORE YOU EXPOSE THEIR SIN, READ THIS: WHAT IF YOU'RE ABOUT TO WOUND SOMEONE JESUS IS TRYING TO RESTORE?
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU EXPOSE THEIR SIN, READ THIS: WHAT IF YOU'RE ABOUT TO WOUND SOMEONE JESUS IS TRYING TO RESTORE?

The Bible never commanded Christians to protect sin. But it never gave us permission to destroy sinners either. Somewhere between public accountability and private correction, the Church is facing a dangerous question: Are we defending the truth of Jesus Christ—or using His name to justify our anger?
One screenshot.
One accusation.
One name exposed.
One post shared thousands of times.
And suddenly, someone's entire life is being discussed by people who have never sat across from them, never heard their side, never prayed with them, and perhaps never even met them.
The comments begin pouring in.
“Expose them!”
“People deserve to know!”
“Stop protecting sinners!”
And somewhere beneath the thousands of reactions, a person is sitting alone, staring at a screen, wondering whether there is any road back from what they have done.
But here is the part that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
What if the person being exposed really did sin?
What if the evidence is undeniable?
What if they are a pastor, a ministry leader, a worship leader, or someone who publicly claims to represent Jesus Christ?
Does love require silence?
Does truth demand exposure?
And if Jesus were standing beside you while you typed that post, would He recognize His heart in your words?
Don't answer too quickly.
Because by the time you finish reading this, you may discover that the greatest danger isn't simply what someone else did wrong.
It may be what happens inside our own hearts when we believe we have the right to punish them.
And Scripture has something to say about that.
Something we cannot afford to ignore.
Jesus said in Matthew 18:15:
“If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.” (KJV)
Read those last four words again.
“Thou hast gained thy brother.”
Not destroyed your brother.
Not humiliated your brother.
Not collected enough screenshots to win an argument.
Gained him.
The Greek expression is ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου (ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou), meaning “you have gained your brother.”
The verb kerdainō carries the sense of gaining or winning something valuable.
Jesus was not teaching His disciples how to win a public confrontation.
He was teaching them to pursue the recovery of someone who had gone wrong.
That changes everything.
Because the goal of biblical correction is not merely to establish that you were right.
It is to seek repentance, restoration, and faithfulness to God.
But there is something else we must understand before turning Matthew 18 into a universal rule for every situation.

In its immediate context, Jesus is teaching about confronting a brother who sins, beginning with a personal approach and escalating when repentance is refused. Matthew 18:15–17 describes private confrontation, witnesses, and eventually telling the matter to the church.
That is a serious process.
But it does not mean every public sin, every case of abuse, every threat to vulnerable people, or every instance of public false teaching must remain private until someone completes those steps.
The Bible is more careful than that.
And Christians must be too.
Imagine a woman sitting in the back row of a church.
She has spent months trying to find the courage to tell someone what a respected leader has done.
She has been told not to damage the ministry.
Not to embarrass the church.
Not to touch the Lord's anointed.
Not to make private matters public.
So she stays silent.
The leader continues preaching.
The congregation continues applauding.
And the person who has been harmed begins to wonder whether God cares more about protecting a reputation than protecting His children.
Now imagine someone approaching her with Matthew 18:15 and telling her she must first confront the person who harmed her alone.
That is not a faithful application of the passage.
It can place someone in further danger.

Scripture never gives church leaders immunity from accountability. Nor does it require victims of abuse or crimes to privately confront an offender before seeking protection, reporting to appropriate authorities, or telling trustworthy people who can help.
Proverbs 31:8 says:
“Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.” (KJV)
The language refers to speaking on behalf of those who cannot effectively speak for themselves.
Sometimes love confronts privately.
Sometimes love warns publicly.
And sometimes love begins by standing beside the person everyone else has pressured into silence.
The difference is not whether the truth is uncomfortable. The difference is whether we are acting faithfully, justly, and lovingly before God.
Consider what happened when the apostle Peter acted inconsistently with the Gospel.
Paul wrote in Galatians 2:11:
“But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.” (KJV)
Then in Galatians 2:14, Paul explained that he spoke to Peter “before them all.”
Why?
Because Peter's conduct had affected others.

His withdrawal from eating with Gentile believers was not merely a private disagreement. His behavior influenced other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, and compromised the truth of the Gospel concerning fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians.
Paul did not remain silent simply because Peter was respected.
He confronted the problem in the setting where it had caused harm.
That matters.
Public wrongdoing with public consequences may require public correction.
Especially when silence would leave people deceived, vulnerable, or spiritually endangered.
But notice something equally important.
Paul confronted Peter's conduct and its contradiction of the Gospel.
The biblical account does not portray Paul encouraging believers to mock Peter, invent accusations, or turn his failure into entertainment.
Paul was defending Gospel truth.
Not building an audience around Peter's humiliation.
There is an enormous difference.
And social media has made that difference frighteningly easy to forget.
Today, we can post a Bible verse while indulging a desire for revenge.
We can call something “discernment” when it is really suspicion.
We can call something “righteous anger” when it is actually wounded pride.
We can call something “exposing darkness” while secretly enjoying the attention the exposure brings.
And the most dangerous part?
We can do all of it while sincerely believing we are serving God.
That is why we need more than confidence.
We need humility.
We need Scripture.
We need the Holy Spirit to examine motives we may not even recognize in ourselves.
James 1:19–20 says:
“Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.” (KJV)
That last sentence should stop our fingers before they touch the keyboard.
Human anger does not produce God's righteousness.
Even when the wrongdoing we are angry about is real.
Even when our concern is justified.
Even when correction is necessary.
Being right about another person's sin does not automatically make our response righteous.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because most of us have stood on both sides of judgment.
We remember times when someone hurt us, lied to us, betrayed us, or misrepresented us.
We know what it feels like to want the world to see what they did.
To want someone to finally say, “You were wronged.”
To want accountability.
And sometimes that desire is legitimate. God is not indifferent to injustice.
But if we are honest, we may also remember something else.
A mistake we made.
A secret we regret.
A season when we were spiritually cold.
A conversation we wish we could take back.
A sin we confessed through tears.
A failure that would have devastated us if the entire internet had been invited to watch.
What if the worst thing you ever did became the only thing people were willing to know about you?
What if your repentance was real, but the screenshots kept circulating?
What if people decided that because you had sinned publicly, you were no longer capable of being changed by grace?
Would that reflect the Gospel?
No.
Because the Gospel does not deny the seriousness of sin.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And this is where we must remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The scribes and Pharisees placed her in the middle of a crowd.
Her sin became the center of public attention.
They asked Jesus what should be done.
But John tells us their purpose was to test Him so they could accuse Him.
They were not merely concerned about righteousness.
They were attempting to use a human being's sin as a weapon against Jesus.
And Jesus responded with words that have echoed through centuries.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV)
The Greek expression ἀναμάρτητος (anamartētos) means “without sin.”
Jesus exposed the moral blindness of those who were eager to condemn while refusing to examine themselves.
One by one, the accusers departed.
But do not misunderstand what happened next.
Jesus did not declare adultery harmless.
He did not celebrate rebellion.
He did not say that repentance was unnecessary.
He told the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And holiness.
Grace.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Together.
Never separated.

There is also an important textual detail worth knowing. The account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Many modern Bibles therefore mark it with a textual note. Christians have long treasured the account, but responsible interpretation should acknowledge its manuscript history rather than conceal it. Its central themes of mercy, moral self-examination, and repentance are also taught clearly elsewhere in Scripture.
And that brings us to a truth no Christian should forget.
Grace is not permission to continue in sin. Grace is God's mercy calling sinners into a transformed life.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts the idea that forgiveness makes sin acceptable.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (KJV)
The Gospel does not tell us to ignore evil.
It tells us that evil is so serious that Jesus Christ bore sin's judgment at the cross, and that God's mercy is so extraordinary that repentant sinners can receive forgiveness through Him.
This is why Christian correction must never become a choice between truth and love.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak “the truth in love.”
In Greek, the expression is ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ (alētheuontes de en agapē).

The verb alētheuō is related to truth and can carry the sense of being truthful or practicing truth. The phrase is broader than merely speaking accurate words; in context, it describes a truth-shaped life within Christian love.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become an excuse.
But truth practiced in love seeks what honors Christ and genuinely serves others.
So what does that mean when a Christian sees public sin on Facebook?
It means we must stop pretending that every situation deserves the same response.
If a fellow believer has personally offended you, and the matter can safely and appropriately be handled between you, Jesus' teaching in Matthew 18 gives a powerful starting point.
Go to the person.
Speak truthfully.
Seek understanding.
Pursue repentance and reconciliation.
Do not make an audience your first destination when a faithful private conversation could resolve the matter.
But if a public teacher is spreading serious false doctrine that is influencing many people, a public biblical response may be necessary.
If a leader's wrongdoing is placing others at risk, protecting people matters more than protecting a public image.
If someone has committed abuse or a crime, safeguarding victims and contacting appropriate authorities must not be delayed by an inappropriate demand for private confrontation.
And if an allegation is circulating without reliable evidence, Christians must refuse to turn uncertainty into a verdict.
Proverbs 18:13 warns against answering a matter before hearing it.
Proverbs 18:17 reminds us that the first account may appear convincing until another person examines it.
These are not minor details.
They are safeguards against injustice.
Because false accusations can destroy lives too.
A viral allegation is not automatically a verified fact.
A screenshot is not always the full story.
A passionate testimony deserves to be taken seriously, but responsible action still requires careful attention to evidence, safety, and fairness.
Protecting the vulnerable and avoiding reckless accusations are not competing biblical duties.
Both matter.
And when public correction is warranted, we must ask what we are trying to accomplish.
Are we warning people about a real danger?
Are we correcting teaching that misrepresents Christ?
Are we helping victims receive protection and justice?
Are we calling someone toward repentance?
Or are we making an example of a sinner because public outrage feels satisfying?
Galatians 6:1 says:
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from katartizō, which can mean to mend, put in order, or restore.
The command does not mean that every person must immediately be returned to leadership, trusted with vulnerable people, or relieved of consequences.
Forgiveness does not erase accountability.
Repentance does not automatically restore lost trust.
A person may be genuinely forgiven by God and still need to step down from ministry, make restitution, submit to lawful consequences, or undergo a long process of rebuilding trust.
Restoration is not the same as reinstatement.
And reconciliation is not the same as removing healthy boundaries.
But the posture of the Christian heart should still matter.
Paul says to restore with meekness.
And to consider yourself.
Why?
Because the person doing the correcting is also a sinner in need of grace.
Not necessarily guilty of the same wrongdoing.
Not equally responsible for the harm.
But still dependent upon the mercy of Jesus Christ.
That truth should make us careful.
Not cowardly.
Careful.
Now consider Paul's instructions concerning elders in 1 Timothy 5:19–20.
He warns against receiving an accusation against an elder without adequate witness testimony, and then says concerning those who continue in sin:
“Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.” (1 Timothy 5:20, KJV)
The passage shows that public accountability can be appropriate, particularly where church leadership is concerned.
It also shows that accusations must be handled responsibly.
Public rebuke is not a license for unverified social media trials.
Church discipline, safeguarding procedures, independent investigation where necessary, lawful reporting, and public communication each have their place.
A faithful response considers the nature of the sin, the evidence, the people affected, the risk of further harm, and the responsibilities of those involved.
Sometimes a private conversation is the wisest first step.
Sometimes immediate protective action is necessary.
Sometimes public correction is justified.
Sometimes the most righteous thing you can do is refuse to share an accusation you cannot verify.
And sometimes silence itself becomes a failure of love.
The question is not simply, “Should I expose this?”
The deeper question is:
“What response would be faithful to Jesus Christ, truthful about the facts, protective of those at risk, and directed toward justice and repentance?”
That question is harder.
It requires more than a reaction.
It requires discipleship.
And perhaps that is why so many of us would rather post.
Posting is fast.
Listening takes time.
Condemning is simple.
Discernment requires patience.
Public outrage can bring immediate approval.
But faithful correction may cost us popularity, relationships, comfort, and even our own reputation.
Jesus never promised that following Him would always make us popular.
He called us to take up our cross.
And that includes refusing to exploit another person's failure for attention.
It also includes refusing to protect powerful people at the expense of those they have harmed.
Both are forms of faithfulness.
Both may require courage.
There is another moment in Scripture that deserves our attention.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Not in a quiet private thought.
Not in an invisible struggle known only to God.
He denied knowing his Lord.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 says that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of the Savior meeting the eyes of the disciple who had just denied Him.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
His sin was not minimized.
But his story was not finished.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus spoke with Peter beside the Sea of Tiberias.
Three times Jesus asked him about his love.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's denial did not become the final chapter of his life.
The risen Christ called him forward.
Now hear this carefully.

Peter's restoration does not mean every fallen leader should be returned to office. His situation was unique, and the qualifications and responsibilities of Christian leadership must still be honored.
But his story does reveal something glorious about Jesus.
The Savior who knows the full truth about our failures is also powerful enough to transform repentant sinners.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not image management.
Not public relations.
Not pretending that sin never happened.
Redemption.
A real Savior meeting real sinners with real grace that calls them into real change.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
Perhaps you are the person who was publicly exposed.
Perhaps you genuinely sinned.
Perhaps you hurt someone.
Perhaps your actions deserve consequences.
And perhaps you are wondering whether you can ever look at yourself the same way again.
Listen.
Do not hide behind grace to avoid repentance.
Do not blame everyone who confronted you.
Do not confuse the discomfort of accountability with persecution.
Confess what you have done.
Turn from it.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept appropriate consequences.
Seek help.
And come to Jesus Christ.
Because the cross is not a hiding place from truth.
It is where sinners can face the truth and discover the mercy of God.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
The Greek word for confess, ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), comes from homologeō, meaning to acknowledge or confess.
Biblical confession is not merely being sorry that people found out.
It is honestly acknowledging sin before God.
And genuine repentance bears fruit in the way we live.
You may not be able to repair every relationship.
You may not recover every opportunity.
You may have to live with consequences that forgiveness does not immediately remove.
But your past does not have to be your master.
Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
And perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
You are the person who was harmed.
Someone used spiritual language to silence you.
Someone demanded that you forgive quickly while refusing to acknowledge what happened.
Someone told you that exposing wrongdoing would damage God's work.
Please hear this.
You are not required to pretend that evil is good.
You are not required to trust someone simply because they say they have repented.
You are not required to abandon wise boundaries to prove you have forgiven.
And seeking protection or justice is not a betrayal of Jesus.
The God who calls sinners to repentance also calls His people to defend the oppressed and act justly.
You matter to Him.
Your safety matters.
The truth matters.
And the name of Jesus should never be used to make you disappear.
Now perhaps there is a third person reading.
The one who has never met the accused.
Never met the victim.
Never investigated the evidence.
But has already shared the post.
Already written the comment.
Already joined the crowd.
Maybe your words were harsher than they needed to be.
Maybe you enjoyed watching someone fall.
Maybe you confused being loud with being faithful.
There is grace for you too.
But grace calls you to repentance as well.
Delete what is false.
Correct what you misrepresented.
Apologize where necessary.
Stop spreading what you do not know.
And before you write another comment in the name of Jesus, remember that every person involved is made in the image of God.
Even the guilty.
Even the wounded.
Even the person with whom you strongly disagree.
The dignity of human beings does not disappear when they sin.
Neither does the necessity of accountability.
This is the narrow road of Christian discipleship.
And it is not easy.
Because the world often demands that we choose a side before we understand the story.
Jesus calls us to something deeper.
Truth without cruelty.
Mercy without compromise.
Justice without vengeance.
Correction without pride.
Forgiveness without denial.
And love that refuses to abandon either holiness or compassion.
That is the kind of Christianity our social media feeds desperately need.
Not Christians who never speak.
Not Christians who expose everyone.
But Christians who have learned to submit their tongues, their keyboards, their anger, and their motives to the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Before you publish that post, imagine bringing it before the Lord.
Can you defend its accuracy?
Have you considered the harm it might cause?
Are you protecting people who need protection?
Have you treated allegations with appropriate care?
Are you speaking because truth and love require it—or because outrage has taken control of your heart?
Would you be willing to correct yourself publicly if you discovered you were wrong?
And if the person you are correcting genuinely repents, will you allow the Gospel to have the final word?
Those questions will not always lead to silence.
Sometimes they will give you the courage to speak when others refuse.
Sometimes they will stop you from posting something destructive.
But they will lead you away from self-righteousness and closer to the heart of Christ.
And that is where Gospel Warrior stands.
Not with a culture that celebrates the destruction of sinners.
Not with a religious system that protects sin behind a polished reputation.
But with the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which calls evil what it is, protects the vulnerable, confronts wrongdoing, proclaims forgiveness, and invites repentant sinners into a transformed life.
From scandal to grace does not mean from scandal to secrecy.
It means bringing what is broken into the light of Christ, where truth is honored, justice is pursued, repentance is real, and grace is never cheapened.
And this is why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters.
Every day, people are being shaped by what they read, watch, believe, and share.
Some are drifting from biblical truth.
Some are carrying wounds inflicted by other Christians.
Some are exhausted from pretending they are spiritually strong.
Some are one honest conversation away from seeking Jesus again.
We want to keep bringing Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, honest conversations, and discipleship resources into those spaces.
Not to build a platform around human personalities.
But to point people toward the One who alone can save.
And please, do not leave without joining this conversation.
What did it teach you about truth and grace?
If this has exposed something in your own heart, you can simply comment, “Lord, teach me to speak truth in love.”
If you are carrying wounds from spiritual mistreatment, you can comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you are still learning how to stand for truth without losing compassion, comment, “Christ is still changing me.”
You do not need to disclose private trauma or another person's identity to participate. Sometimes the most meaningful testimony begins with a few honest words.
Giving should never be forced, manipulated, or treated as a purchase of God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the kind of support we welcome.
Freely given.
Prayerfully considered.
Motivated by love for Christ and a desire to help His Word reach others.
Your generosity can be one practical way to participate in this mission, alongside prayer, faithful service, and sharing the Gospel with people around you.
Pray for the ministry.
Send it privately to a friend who is wrestling with a difficult question about faith.
And keep growing in the Word of God.
It is to see people become faithful disciples of Jesus Christ.
One day, the arguments on our timelines will fade.
The trending controversies will disappear.
The applause will stop.
The angry comments will be forgotten.
But we will still answer to the Lord for how we handled the truth He entrusted to us.
So when another Christian falls, do not rush to become their executioner.
When someone is harmed, do not rush to become the defender of the powerful.
When accusations arise, do not confuse suspicion with proof.
When repentance is genuine, do not act as though Christ is powerless to change a life.
And when truth must be spoken publicly, speak it with the courage of someone who fears God more than public opinion.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become experts at destroying one another.
He died and rose again to redeem sinners, create a holy people, and teach us to walk in truth and love.
The next time your finger hovers over the Share button, remember this:
Someone's reputation may be at stake.
Someone's safety may be at stake.
Someone's faith may be trembling.
And your witness to Jesus Christ is always at stake.
Never protect sin in the name of grace. Never destroy a soul in the name of truth. And never forget that the same cross that exposes our guilt also reveals the Savior who can redeem us.
